questions.prompt: What does plan mode change about how Claude Code works?

options.text: It makes Claude respond faster by skipping analysis
Claude explores read-only and must present a plan for your approval before making any changes
It disables all tools including reading

questions.explanation: Plan mode separates research from execution: read and think freely, change nothing, get sign-off on the approach first.

questions.prompt: Which task most deserves plan mode?

options.text: Fixing an obvious typo in a README
Renaming a function used in one file
Restructuring how authentication flows through a 40-file codebase you don't know well

questions.explanation: Plan mode earns its overhead when changes are broad, the codebase is unfamiliar, or a wrong start is expensive. Trivial edits don't need a signed plan.

questions.prompt: Beyond safety, what does plan-first working buy you? (select all that apply)

options.text: The plan is a compact artifact — you can carry it into a fresh session and discard the messy exploration
You catch a wrong approach at the cheapest possible moment: before any code changed
It guarantees the plan will execute without bugs
You can edit the plan to steer execution before it starts

questions.explanation: A plan is both a safety gate and a context artifact — the summarize-then-restart pattern built into the workflow. No guarantee of bug-free execution, though (c).

title: Terminal: Read-Only Planning
instructions: Claude has NO write tools here — a plan-mode stance enforced by permissions. The project has a deliberately tangled utils.js where three functions duplicate date-formatting logic. Ask: 'Study this project and write a step-by-step plan to remove the duplicated date logic, without changing any files. Number the steps, list which files each touches, and flag any risks.' Review the plan like a tech lead: is the order right? Did it miss the usage in report.js? Push back with a follow-up if so — refining a plan is the point of planning.
